doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Learning tunes on the bandstand; Lou Donaldson and jazz education
summary: Jazz education over-emphasizes reading; Weiss recalls George Coleman and Lou Donaldson springing tunes on him, and finding clues in the bass line.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Is that something you try to pass on to jazz majors in college? The fact that those years that you played at that level that you were playing from intuition and memory?

I mean yes of course. That’s the biggest problem — probably one of the most fundamental problems with jazz education is an emphasis on reading music and not using your ear and not pulling the music away. But so much of this has to do with the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

professional experience. You know there’s so fewer opportunities for younger players to work, to play, to perform on a regular basis, to apprentice with established players, to have to kind of sink or swim in that, on the bandstand so to speak. Those skills are just gone away. You know? If there were a lot more performing opportunities with a — that were still using the Great American Songbook you know, young sidemen would just have to buckle down and be able to learn and hear songs that they didn’t know on the bandstand. I’ve experienced that throughout my career. Every time I get on the bandstand with George Coleman I’m going to learn a new song. Lou Donaldson. You know like Lou would never announce a song before he plays it. He never counted a song off before he started to play it. He never tapped his foot into a song, he just started playing the melody of the song he wanted to play in tempo and you were expected to know it. One time he — we were playing a gig in Connecticut and he started to play [scats] and Jamil Nasser is playing and the drummer is playing. And I’m like, I’m frozen. I don’t know what that is. And he turned around and he looked at me, he says, “Ha you don’t know that man? A-ha-ha-ha.” And I learned it, by a chorus I had it. It was a song called “You.” Sonny Rollins recorded it. But that’s how you learn.
Does it help because you had perfect pitch that you can listen to the bass player and that’s vital what the bass player is playing, especially if you don’t know a tune.
Well you better hope the bass player knows it. What do you do if he doesn’t know it either? You’re making assumptions there.
Really. The bass player is sneaking over to look at your left hand and you’re going, “Sorry.”

Yeah. So you have to get your clues from wherever you can find them. Obviously the more songs you know the more ways you know a harmonic progression might likely go, or what chords a melody is implying by the tonality that the melody is in at the moment.
